name: Reconnaissance Brigade
doctrine_source: ATP 7-100.1, para 4-72, p.4-24 (separate reconnaissance brigade -- razvedyvatelnaya brigada, known as Pb -- a separate brigade at the operational echelon; organic capabilities include long-range reconnaissance, long-range sensor reconnaissance, intelligence and electromagnetic warfare, and mounted and dismounted reconnaissance, plus extensive UAVs; may be augmented by selectively task-organized mechanized, armor, antitank, artillery, air defense, sniper, engineer, aviation and air assault support -- those augmentations are task-organized, not organic). Existence and parent confirmed as an organic combined-arms (group) army asset in T2COM G-2 How Russia Fights in LSCO, fig 6 (Russian Ground Forces Group Army Structure), p.12. No subordinate-unit org chart or TO&E table is charted for this brigade in any swept source (ATP 7-100.1 fig list, TC 7-100.4 App A, DIA Russia Military Power 2017, How Russia Fights); root node only, no echeloned subunits invented.

name: Air Defense Brigade (Combined Arms Army)
doctrine_source: ATP 7-100.1, para 4-156, 4-160, 4-167, p.4-39 to p.4-40 (the Air Defense Brigades of the Combined Arms Armies field BUK-M1 (SA-11 Gadfly) and BUK-M2 (SA-17 Grizzly) medium-range surface-to-air missile complexes at the strategic-operational echelon; the army echelon allocates subunits from the air defense brigade to subordinate divisions to build the IADS; SA-11 gives 30 km coverage to 14 km altitude and is being replaced by SA-17, 70 km to 35 km; air defense is automated across regiments, brigades, battalions, and batteries). Existence and parent confirmed as an organic combined-arms (group) army asset in T2COM G-2 How Russia Fights in LSCO, fig 6, p.12, and DIA Russia Military Power 2017, p.53 (the combined arms army includes air defense units). No subordinate-battalion org chart or TO&E table for the army air defense brigade is charted in any swept source; the medium-range SAM equipment it fields is recorded on the root node.

name: Engineer Brigade (Army)
doctrine_source: ATP 7-100.1, Appendix G, para G-1 to G-5, p.G-1 to p.G-2 (engineer brigades are army-level assets; the standard SV engineer battalion carries, in its route-construction / movement-support detachment role, four BAT-2 combat engineer vehicles, two DZ-180A road grader/scrapers, two KRAZ-257B wheeled cranes, and four TMM-3 truck-launched bridge sets; the GMZ-3 tracked mine layer -- three per SV obstacle platoon -- is assigned to engineer brigades (army level) and engineer regiments (military-district level)). Existence corroborated in T2COM G-2 How Russia Fights in LSCO, p.12 (the army-group engineer element is charted there as an engineering REGIMENT, with pontoon bridge brigades separate) and DIA Russia Military Power 2017, p.53 (the combined arms army includes engineer units). No brigade-echelon org chart is charted in any swept source; the engineer battalion and obstacle platoon shown are the documented building blocks with verbatim per-unit equipment counts -- the number of battalions per brigade is not stated by any source.

name: Army Aviation Combat Helicopter Regiment
doctrine_source: ATP 7-100.1, para 5-129 to 5-139, p.5-40 to p.5-41, and Table C-2 (rotary-wing aircraft characteristics), p.C-4. Army aviation (Aviatsiya Sukhoputnykh Voysk, ASV) rotary-wing forces are organized as aviation REGIMENTS -- the primary administrative and tactical structure -- not as brigades in any swept source; each aviation regiment has several subordinate aviation (combat) squadrons plus an engineering-services squadron, squadrons being made of two to three detachments of three to four aircraft (para 5-136), and combat aircraft regiments typically consist of two squadrons with four aircraft each (p.7466 context); during competition the army aviation unit at the military-district permanent airbase consists of command and control, combat squadrons, and a technical (TEC) squadron (para 5-139). Attack helicopter types per Table C-2: Mi-28NE, Mi-24 / Mi-35, Ka-52; transport/assault: Mi-8 / Mi-17, Mi-26. Requested as a combat helicopter brigade; recorded at the echelon the sources actually chart (Regiment). The battalion-echelon Typical Tactical Helicopter Aviation Unit (fig 5-28, p.5-41) is captured separately as rus_tactical_helicopter_aviation_unit.

name: Air Assault Brigade (VDV)
doctrine_source: DIA Russia Military Power 2017, The Airborne Troops, p.55 to p.56 (the VDV comprises four maneuver divisions, four air assault brigades -- the 11th, 31st, 56th, and 83rd -- and one separate special-purpose (Spetsnaz) reconnaissance brigade, the 45th; VDV maneuver formations are designated either parachute or air assault; the VDV Primary Combat Vehicles table lists BMD-2 (IFV), BMD-4M (IFV), BTR-D (tracked APC), BTR-MDM (tracked APC), 2S9 120-mm SP combination gun, and 2S25 125-mm tracked SP antitank gun; in late 2016 the air assault brigades received up to a company (10 to 13) of T-72-series main battle tanks, planned to grow to tank battalions (30 to 42)). Corroborated by ATP 7-100.1, Appendix K, para K-16 and K-17, p.K-3 to p.K-4 (VDV organization and capabilities are similar to other combined-arms units; the VDV also uses the 2S9 Nona-S 120mm SP mortar and the BTR-ZD anti-aircraft gun; Table K-1 counts the VDV as four divisions, five brigades, ~45,000). No subordinate-battalion org chart or TO&E table is charted for a VDV air assault brigade in any swept source; the tank company is the only discrete subunit any source names for the brigade; the air-droppable brigade equipment set is recorded on the root node. Source charts an AIR ASSAULT brigade type (not a parachute brigade).
